title: Testing: checking that code does what you meant
summary: Write assertions and unittest test cases, choose the edge cases that catch real bugs, and judge your tests by whether they catch broken code.
license: Original work for Python Intelligence; license to be chosen by the owner
objective: Write tests that pass on correct code and fail on broken code, choosing the edge cases where bugs hide.
analogy: Tests are a smoke detector: one that never goes off isn't proof there's no fire, so you test it with smoke (broken code) to see it sound.

misconceptions.belief: If all my tests pass, the code is correct.
misconceptions.correction: Passing tests show only the cases they try; a good suite would fail on likely bugs.

misconceptions.belief: A test only needs the obvious example.
misconceptions.correction: Bugs hide at edges: empty input, boundaries, repeats and unusual spacing.

misconceptions.belief: The first line of a traceback shows where the error happened.
misconceptions.correction: The last frame, just above the message, is where it was raised.

rubric.evidence: each likely bug makes at least one test fail
no test fails on a correct implementation
empty, single and unusual inputs are covered

review.recall: How can you tell whether a test suite is any good? Which part of a traceback names the line that raised?

steps.title: "It works on my example"
steps.body:
You write a function, try it on one input, see the right answer and move on. A week later a classmate
calls it with an empty list, or a negative number, or the value right on a boundary, and it breaks. A
**test** is a small program that checks your code for you, on the cases you might forget, every time
you change it. Good tests are what let you change code without fear.

steps.title: A test is only as good as the bugs it catches
steps.body:
An **assertion** states something that must be true: `assert total >= 0, 'total went negative'` stops the
program with an `AssertionError` if it isn't. A **unit test** calls one function with a chosen input and
asserts the expected output; the `unittest` module collects many such tests, runs them and reports
failures.

Passing tests prove little on their own: a test that only tries `clamp(5, 0, 10)` passes for plenty of
wrong code. The real question is *would this test fail if the code were wrong?* So test the **edge
cases** where bugs hide: the boundaries themselves, empty and one-element inputs, negative numbers,
inputs in an unusual order, and the errors bad input should raise.

questions: Which single test would catch a clamp that forgets the upper limit?
Why is `clamp(10, 0, 10)` a better test than `clamp(7, 0, 10)`?

steps.title: The precise rules
steps.body:
**Assertions:** `assert condition, message` raises `AssertionError(message)` when the condition is false.
Use them for things that must never happen; Python can run with assertions switched off (`python -O`),
so don't use them to validate user input in real programs.

**unittest:** a test case is a class that inherits from `unittest.TestCase`; each method whose name starts
with `test` is one test. Inside, `self.assertEqual(a, b)` fails unless `a == b`, `self.assertTrue(x)` unless
`x` is truthy, and `with self.assertRaises(ValueError):` fails unless the indented code raises that error.
`unittest.main()` (or a loader and a runner) finds and runs the tests and reports failures (an assertion
failed) and errors (an unexpected exception).

**Choosing tests:** one test per behaviour; the boundaries and just beyond them; empty and single inputs;
the errors that bad input must raise; and a check that inputs aren't changed when they shouldn't be.

**Tests first:** write the test before the code. Run it and watch it *fail* (red): that shows it can
detect the missing behaviour. Then write just enough code to make it pass (green), and tidy up with the
test as a safety net (refactor).

**Reading a traceback:** Python prints the calls that were active when the error happened, *most recent
call last*. The last line names the error and its message; the frame just above it is the line that
raised it; the frames above that show who called whom. The fix often belongs in an earlier frame, where
the bad value came from.

steps.title: Run it: read a traceback, frame by frame
steps.body:
`report` averages each group, and one group is empty. Instead of letting the error stop the program, this
catches it and lists the traceback's frames, oldest first: the call at the bottom of the program, then
`report`, then `average`, where the division failed. The empty list was passed in by `report`.
steps.expected_output:
line 10 in <module>
line 7 in report
line 4 in average
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

steps.title: Your turn: tests that catch bugs
steps.body:
`clamp(x, lo, hi)` returns `x` limited to the range `lo..hi` (inclusive), and raises `ValueError` if `lo > hi`.
The starter gives you a correct `clamp`. Complete `TestClamp`, a `unittest.TestCase`, so that every test
passes on the correct `clamp`, and so that at least one test fails on each of several broken versions
(which the checks will swap in for `clamp`). Think about the boundaries, a range below zero, a range of a
single value, and the error.
hints: Test `clamp(0, 0, 10)` and `clamp(10, 0, 10)`: values exactly on the limits catch off-by-one bugs.
Use `with self.assertRaises(ValueError): clamp(1, 10, 0)` to require the error.

steps.title: Your turn: follow the traceback to the fix
steps.body:
`report(groups)` should give each group's average, rounded to one decimal place, and `None` for an empty
group. Run the checks: `report([[2, 4], [], [5]])` crashes, and the failed check shows the traceback's frames,
most recent call last. Which function raised the error, and which caller passed the bad value in? Fix the code so that the checks pass, and keep `average` raising for
an empty list (that is a reasonable thing for `average` to do).
hints: The last line is ZeroDivisionError in `average`; the frame above it is `report`, which passed it an empty group.
Fix it where the empty group comes in: `round(average(g), 1) if g else None`.

tests.name: an empty group gives None
ordinary groups are averaged and rounded
average still refuses an empty list

steps.title: Challenge: write the tests first
steps.body:
`median(xs)` should return the middle value of the sorted numbers, or the mean of the two middle values when
there is an even count; raise `ValueError` for an empty list; and not change `xs`. Write
`check_median(median)`, which takes *some* implementation and returns quietly if it is correct, but raises an
exception (normally an `AssertionError`) if it gets any of those rules wrong. This is writing the tests
first: you pin down what `median` must do before seeing any version of it. The checks then give your
function a correct median and several broken ones.
hints: Try an unsorted list, an even-length list whose middle values average to a fraction, and an empty list.
To require an exception: `try: median([])`, `except ValueError: pass`, `else: raise AssertionError(...)`.

def check_median(median):
    assert median([3]) == 3, 'one value is its own median'
    assert median([5, 1, 3]) == 3, 'sort before taking the middle'
    assert median([4, 1, 3, 2]) == 2.5, 'an even count averages the two middle values'
    assert median([1, 2]) == 1.5, 'not integer division'
    assert median([-4, -1, -7]) == -4, 'negative numbers'
    assert median([1, 2, 10]) == 2, 'the middle value, not the mean'
    data = [9, 2, 7]
    median(data)
    assert data == [9, 2, 7], 'the input list must not change'
    try:
        median([])
    except ValueError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError('an empty list must raise ValueError')

catches a median that doesn't sort

steps.solution:
def check_median(median):
    assert median([3]) == 3, 'one value is its own median'
    assert median([5, 1, 3]) == 3, 'sort before taking the middle'
    assert median([4, 1, 3, 2]) == 2.5, 'an even count averages the two middle values'
    assert median([1, 2]) == 1.5, 'not integer division'
    assert median([-4, -1, -7]) == -4, 'negative numbers'
    assert median([1, 2, 10]) == 2, 'the middle value, not the mean'
    data = [9, 2, 7]
    median(data)
    assert data == [9, 2, 7], 'the input list must not change'
    try:
        median([])
    except ValueError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError('an empty list must raise ValueError')

steps.title: Transfer: tests for a word counter
steps.body:
`word_count(text)` returns the number of words in `text`, where words are separated by any whitespace (spaces, tabs or
newlines, one or more), punctuation stays part of its word, and an empty or blank string has 0 words. The starter
gives you a correct version. Complete `TestWordCount` so that every test passes on it and at least one fails on each
of several broken versions the checks will swap in.
hints: Try an empty string, double spaces, a tab or newline, and punctuation like "Hi, there."
One method can hold several assertEqual lines; what matters is that each bug fails somewhere.

tests.name: your tests pass on the correct word_count
tests.code:
import unittest

def _run(impl):
    global word_count
    saved = word_count
    word_count = impl
    try:
        suite = unittest.defaultTestLoader.loadTestsFromTestCase(TestWordCount)
        result = unittest.TestResult()
        suite.run(result)
        return result.testsRun, len(result.failures) + len(result.errors)
    finally:
        word_count = saved

ran, bad = _run(lambda text: len(text.split()))
assert ran >= 1, 'TestWordCount has no test methods yet: name each one test_something'
assert bad == 0, f'{bad} of your tests fail on a correct word_count'

questions.prompt: Which test best catches a clamp that returns hi - 1 for values at or above hi?
questions.explanation: Only a value at the limit itself exercises that boundary.

questions.prompt: A test suite passes on your code. What does that prove?
choices: Only that the code handles the cases the tests try
That the code has no bugs
That the tests are complete
Nothing at all
questions.explanation: Tests show the presence of the behaviours they check, not the absence of every bug.

choices: That the indented code raises ValueError
That no ValueError happens
That the test is skipped on ValueError
That ValueError is caught and ignored
questions.explanation: The test fails if the block finishes without raising that error.

questions.prompt: Why not rely on assert to validate user input in a real program?
choices: Assertions can be switched off with python -O
assert is slower than if
assert only works in tests
assert can't show a message
questions.explanation: Use assertions for 'this can't happen' checks; validate input with if and raise.

questions.prompt: Writing a test first, what should it do the first time you run it, before you write the code?
choices: Fail, showing it can detect the missing behaviour
Pass, to prove the test is correct
Raise a SyntaxError
Be skipped until the code exists
questions.explanation: A new test that passes before the code exists can't be testing that code. Red first, then green.

questions.prompt: In a Python traceback, where is the line that actually raised the error?
choices: In the last frame, just above the error message
In the first frame at the top
In the frame that calls print
Tracebacks don't show it
questions.explanation: Tracebacks list the most recent call last; the cause of the bad value is often in an earlier frame.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.body:
- State assumptions with `assert` and read an `AssertionError`.
- Write a `unittest.TestCase` with `assertEqual` and `assertRaises`, and run it.
- Choose edge cases: boundaries, empty and single inputs, negatives, errors, unchanged inputs.
- Judge tests by whether they would fail on broken code.
- Write a test first, watch it fail, then make it pass.
- Read a traceback from the bottom up, and fix the cause where the bad value came from.
